---
title: "Changepoint Detection"
subtitle: "Specific Conductance — a level shift at an unknown point"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(strucchange)
library(lmtest)
source("R/utils.R")
non_linear_wq <- readr::read_csv("data/synthetic/non_linear_wq.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cond <- non_linear_wq |> filter(analyte == "Specific Conductance")
```

## What changepoint detection is

Piecewise regression (previous chapter) assumes a slope on at least one side of the knot and asks how much it changes. Specific Conductance doesn't fit that setup: it holds at one level, then jumps to another, with no slope — flat — on either side. Testing for a slope change would find nothing, because there isn't one; the thing that changed is the mean itself.

That's the piecewise-constant case from the previous chapter's three-stage progression — each segment gets its own flat mean, no slope term at all — with one difference: there the knot was known and given as a `cut()` point, here it isn't. Changepoint detection is what that stage becomes once the knot's location has to be found rather than assumed.

**Why a segment's mean counts as an OLS fit.** `lm(y ~ 1)` on a set of points estimates one coefficient, the intercept, by minimizing the sum of squared residuals $\sum (y_i - \hat\beta_0)^2$. Differentiate with respect to $\hat\beta_0$, set it to zero, and the minimizer is $\hat\beta_0 = \bar y$ — the sample mean. So "each segment's mean is fit by OLS" isn't a loose analogy: an intercept-only regression on a subset of points and the arithmetic mean of that subset are the same number, arrived at by the same minimization, just described two different ways. `lm(log(result) ~ period)` in the Results section below does the same thing with one more coefficient — a shared baseline plus an offset for the second segment — still fit by minimizing squared residuals, which is why it's still legitimate to call this a regression rather than a two-sample test dressed up as one.

**Stated as a model.** For a single break at position $\tau$ in the observation sequence, the flat-mean version of this is

$$y_i = \mu_1 \, \mathbb{1}(i \le \tau) + \mu_2 \, \mathbb{1}(i > \tau) + \varepsilon_i,$$

two segment means and an indicator for which segment each observation falls in — exactly the `lm(log(result) ~ period)` fit in the Results section below, once $\tau$ is known. The estimation problem is finding $\hat\tau$ itself:

$$\hat\tau = \arg\min_{\tau} \; \mathrm{RSS}(\tau), \qquad \mathrm{RSS}(\tau) = \sum_{i \le \tau} (y_i - \bar y_{\le \tau})^2 + \sum_{i > \tau} (y_i - \bar y_{> \tau})^2,$$

the split point whose two segment means leave the smallest total squared residual, out of every admissible split. What `strucchange::breakpoints()` adds on top of that is doing this search automatically: it fits the OLS regression at every admissible location (via the dynamic-programming algorithm of Bai and Perron, 2003) and returns whichever minimizes $\mathrm{RSS}(\tau)$, rather than requiring a location — or even a starting guess near one, as `segmented()` does — to be supplied up front.

**If a slope had been present on either side instead, this would look different.** An intercept-only fit assumes a flat mean within each segment; if the data actually trended up or down within a segment, that flat line wouldn't track it, and the leftover trend would typically show up as a violation in the diagnostics below (autocorrelated or trending residuals) or as one segment's fit visibly missing the data on one side. `breakpoints()` doesn't require assuming the answer either way — it accepts any regression formula, so `breakpoints(log(result) ~ year_frac)` fits a non-continuous piecewise-*linear* model instead, a slope and intercept per segment, with the knot still found by search. The "Locating it" section below runs both and lets BIC decide, rather than assuming a flat mean is right: if slopes actually mattered here, the slope-and-intercept form would win, and the write-up would report two rates the way the piecewise chapter does, instead of one level jump.

**The point of doing any of this.** The output this analysis exists to produce is the same shape of answer as the piecewise chapter's — is there a real break, where is it, and how big is it — with a formal test behind each piece rather than an eyeballed read: a significance test for whether a break exists at all (`sctest()` below), a location with a confidence interval, and a percentage change in level with its own p-value, the same "did conductance step up, when, and by how much" a client or regulator would ask about a suspected operational change. The situation it's built for is a suspected step change with an unrecorded date — an operational change, a new discharge starting, a permit-limit revision, a lab or method switch — where there's reason to think something shifted but no on-record date to seed a local search with. `segmented()` needs a plausible starting guess close to the true knot to converge correctly; an exhaustive search over every candidate split doesn't, which makes it the better first-pass tool for an undocumented shift, or for screening many series at once without eyeballing each one first.

## The shape in the record

```{r}
#| label: cond-raw-series
#| message: false
ggplot(cond, aes(year_frac, log(result))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Specific Conductance — log scale") +
  nlt_theme
```

Flat, then a step up, with no visible slope change on either side of the jump.

## Is there a break at all

Before locating anything, it's worth testing whether a break is there at all, rather than assuming one and going straight to where. The **`supF` test** scans every candidate split point and asks whether the best of them fits meaningfully better than a single flat mean across the whole record.

```{r}
#| label: cond-fstats
fs <- Fstats(log(result) ~ 1, data = cond)
sctest(fs, type = "supF")
```

The test rejects the no-break null decisively ($p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$): some split in the record explains the data far better than treating it as one constant mean throughout.

## Locating it, and choosing the right form

`breakpoints()` fits the optimal partition for a given number of breaks, and BIC across increasing break counts picks how many to keep. Run against two candidate forms — a flat mean per segment, and a slope-and-intercept per segment — to check whether the added flexibility of a piecewise-*linear* fit is actually earning its keep here.

```{r}
#| label: cond-breakpoints
bp_mean <- breakpoints(log(result) ~ 1, data = cond)
bp_slope <- breakpoints(log(result) ~ year_frac, data = cond)

summary(bp_mean)
summary(bp_slope)
```

Both forms select the same single breakpoint at observation 87, and both agree it's the best choice of break count — BIC turns up sharply from 0 to 1 break and creeps back up after. The forms disagree on whether that break should carry a slope: at one break, the flat-mean model's BIC (-397.3) is lower than the slope-and-intercept model's (-387.6). Adding two slope parameters costs more in complexity than it recovers in fit, which is the data-driven version of what the raw plot already suggested — this is a *level shift*, not a change in trend. The flat-mean model, `bp_mean`, is carried forward.

## Results

```{r}
#| label: cond-confint
ci <- confint(bp_mean)
ci
brk_idx <- ci$confint[, "breakpoints"]
cond$year_frac[ci$confint[, c("2.5 %", "breakpoints", "97.5 %")]]
```

The breakpoint falls at observation 87, `year_frac` ≈ 7.16 (95% CI 7.08–7.25) — a little over seven years into the twelve-year record. `strucchange`'s convention is that the reported observation is the last one belonging to the *first* segment, so the split is applied as strictly-after that index below.

```{r}
#| label: cond-segment-means
period <- factor(seq_along(cond$year_frac) > brk_idx, labels = c("before", "after"))
fit <- lm(log(result) ~ period, data = cond)
summary(fit)

means <- tapply(log(cond$result), period, mean)
exp(means)
pct_jump <- (exp(diff(means)) - 1) * 100
pct_jump
```

The mean level rises from about 299 to about 422 (units of the raw analyte), a jump of roughly 41%, and the coefficient on `periodafter` is far from zero ($p < 2\times10^{-16}$).

```{r}
#| label: cond-fitted-plot
cond_pred <- cond |> mutate(fitted = predict(fit))
brk_year <- cond$year_frac[brk_idx]
ci_years <- cond$year_frac[ci$confint[, c("2.5 %", "97.5 %")]]

ggplot(cond, aes(year_frac, log(result))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ci_years[1], xmax = ci_years[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = cond_pred, aes(y = fitted, group = period), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = brk_year, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = brk_year, y = max(log(cond$result)),
    label = sprintf("break = %.2f yr, jump = %.1f%%", brk_year, pct_jump),
    hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.2
  ) +
  labs(title = "Specific Conductance — mean-shift fit (log scale)") +
  nlt_theme
```

## Model diagnostics

The two-segment fit is still an OLS regression, so the same assumptions apply: homoscedasticity and normally distributed residuals (see [Transformations](transformations.qmd)).

```{r}
#| label: cond-bptest
bptest(fit)
```

```{r}
#| label: cond-shapiro
shapiro.test(resid(fit))
```

Both tests fail to reject their null: the Breusch-Pagan test ($p = 0.286$) finds no evidence of heteroscedasticity, and the Shapiro-Wilk test ($p = 0.889$) finds no evidence of non-normal residuals.

Neither test checks independence, and monthly data has an obvious way to fail it:

```{r}
#| label: cond-acf
acf(resid(fit), main = "Specific Conductance — residual autocorrelation")
Box.test(resid(fit), lag = 1, type = "Ljung-Box")
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation is close to zero and the Ljung-Box test finds no evidence against independence ($p = 0.368$). All three assumptions hold, supporting the fit as a defensible basis for the interpretation below.

## Interpretation

Specific Conductance held at a stable level for the first seven-plus years of the record, then stepped up to a new, equally stable level, with the shift located — not assumed — at `year_frac` ≈ 7.16 (95% CI 7.08–7.25). Unlike the piecewise-regression case, no slope was fit or needed on either side of the break: comparing a flat-mean model against a slope-and-intercept one at the same breakpoint showed the added slope terms cost more in model complexity than they recovered in fit, confirming this is a level shift rather than a change in trend. The jump itself is large and precisely estimated — the mean level rises by roughly 41%, from about 299 to about 422 — and the diagnostics support treating the two-segment fit as a defensible basis for that reading.

## Extending this analysis

Locating the break statistically is only half of what a regulator or client actually wants — the next step is attribution: checking the estimated date (`year_frac` ≈ 7.16, roughly year 2020) against operational logs, permit modifications, or upstream discharge records to see what happened around then. Nothing in this analysis can supply that on its own; the break's confidence interval narrows where to look, not why it happened. If several analytes or several monitoring sites are believed to share a common cause, it's also worth testing whether the same breakpoint shows up in more than one series at once — `breakpoints()` fits each series independently here, but a shared-cause hypothesis is really a claim about a common changepoint across series, which calls for a joint test rather than eyeballing whether several independently-estimated dates happen to be close.
